analysis.file_name: Unexpected employment slowdown supports Fed pause in October   - 2026-10-02.pdf
analysis.title: Unexpected employment slowdown supports Fed pause in October
key_insights: September nonfarm payrolls grew only 29k against a median estimate of 90k and a consensus range of 35k to 180k. August was revised to 133k from 162k, and the two-month downward revision totals 60k.

Unemployment rose to 4.2% from 4.1% because the participation rate rose to 61.8%, reversing part of this year's downward trend in participation. SEB says this should ease any concern that labour demand could force companies to raise pay.

Hourly earnings growth slowed to 3.0% y/y from 3.1%. SEB says that with productivity growth of 2% y/y or more, wages are not an inflation threat. It treats the quarterly Employment Cost Index as the more reliable wage measure, and that index gives the same message.

SEB says the Fed need not read the slowdown as labour market weakness. Stricter immigration policy and an aging population lower the break-even pace of job growth. The 3-month average of about 50k sits inside estimates of a new 30k to 60k monthly break-even.
A Fed staff analysis earlier this year concluded that months with negative employment changes could become normal under the lower break-even.

SEB says the data supports Vice Chairs Williams and Jefferson, who argue the Fed could take time to evaluate the September hike. August's strong jobs print had been read by many at the Fed as a sign that policy is not restrictive enough, and that reading is less clear after this report.
Composition is weaker. Government jobs fell 17k and private health care and social assistance added 23k. Non-cyclical employment was little changed at +3k, so it is no longer the driver of hiring.

Cyclical sectors are also weakening. Information lost 10k jobs and financial activities lost 7k, which SEB says could signal an AI effect. Temporary health services fell 11k, a generally weak sign because temporary workers are where firms usually start cutting. Leisure and entertainment added 10k after volatile summer readings that may reflect the World Cup.

SEB cautions against drawing conclusions from one month. Employment data is volatile and often revised, and September had an unusually low survey response rate. It describes the market as back in a low-hire, low-fire pattern with sluggish hiring and very low layoffs.

Markets cut the probability of an October hike to about 20% (5 bp) and still fully price a December hike (25 bp accumulated). Three additional hikes are priced across 2026 and 2027 after the September increase.
SEB keeps its forecast of one more Fed hike in December and a return to cuts in late 2027, and sees no reason to change that view because of this report.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Well below the 90k median estimate and below the bottom of the 35k to 180k consensus range. SEB sees it as consistent with a lower break-even pace of job growth and as support for an October Fed pause.
The median pre-release estimate. The actual print missed it by 61k.
The August revision plus another revision to earlier months total 60k downward. This weakens the strong August reading that had pushed some Fed members toward more tightening.

Up from 4.1% and above the unchanged-at-4.1% estimate. It reflects a rise in participation. SEB says it is still consistent with the Fed's view of a stable labour market and eases overheating concerns.
Above the 61.6% estimate. Normally a sign of labour market strength, but it follows a steady downward trend this year.
Down from 3.1% and below the 3.1% estimate. With productivity growth of 2% y/y or more, SEB sees no inflation risk from wages.

macro_indicators.reading: 0.1% in the key points, 0.2% in the body text
macro_indicators.interpretation: The report gives two different monthly figures. Both are below the 0.3% estimate and below the prior 0.3%.

macro_indicators.indicator: Market-implied probability of October Fed hike
macro_indicators.interpretation: Market pricing after the report, lowered further. A December hike remains fully priced.

macro_indicators.reading: one more hike in December 2026, cuts resuming in late 2027
macro_indicators.interpretation: SEB leaves its call unchanged by the report, which makes it more hawkish than a pause-and-cut reading of the data.

risk_factors: The September payroll figure may be unreliable. Payrolls are volatile and often revised, and the survey response rate was unusually low.
Earlier strong activity data, including August employment, may mean policy is not restrictive enough, which would keep the Fed on a hiking path.
Job losses in information and financial activities, and a decline in temporary health services, could mark broader cyclical labour weakness.
Hourly earnings are not adjusted for changes in worker mix and can be distorted by calendar effects tied to the survey week.
vol_and_positioning: Rates market positioning after the report: the October hike probability fell to about 20% (5 bp), a December hike is fully priced at 25 bp accumulated, and three more hikes are priced across 2026 and 2027.
geopolitical: Stricter immigration policies and deportations are cited as lowering the break-even pace of US employment growth.
The World Cup is cited as a possible reason for volatile leisure and entertainment hiring over the summer.

tension_points.bull_case: The 29k payroll print, 60k of downward revisions, a higher unemployment rate and slower wage growth reduce the case for tightening further. Vice Chairs Williams and Jefferson already favour taking time to evaluate the September hike.
tension_points.bear_case: The weak print may not reflect weakness. The break-even pace of job growth is now put at 30k to 60k a month, the 3-month average is about 50k, payrolls are volatile, and the response rate was unusually low. SEB still forecasts a December hike and the market fully prices one.

theme_stances.key_argument: The weak September jobs report and downward revisions support those at the Fed who want time to evaluate the September hike.
theme_stances.evidence: the Fed could take time to evaluate the September hike

theme_stances.theme: labour market not an inflation risk
theme_stances.key_argument: Higher unemployment and slower earnings growth against productivity growth of 2% or more mean the labour market is not an inflation source now.
theme_stances.evidence: the labour market is not a source of inflation at present
